steps.title: Spinal Cord and Spinal Meninges
steps.body: The spinal cord continues from the medulla and gives rise to spinal nerves through dorsal and ventral roots. Its meninges are continuous with cranial meninges, but the spinal epidural space is a real fat-filled venous space.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Spinal cord ends around L1-L2 in adults as conus medullaris. Cauda equina consists of lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal roots below the cord termination. Denticulate ligaments anchor spinal cord laterally to dura. Filum terminale extends inferiorly from conus region. The lumbar cistern extends below the usual adult cord termination and contains cauda equina roots in CSF; this spatial relation explains commonly discussed lumbar access levels.

steps.title: Why is a vertebral level not identical to a spinal cord segment in the lower back?
steps.body: During growth the vertebral column lengthens more than the spinal cord. Lower cord segments therefore lie above the correspondingly named vertebrae, and their roots descend within the canal before exiting. The conus is the tapering cord end, while cauda equina consists of roots below it. A vertebral injury can affect a different segment than its bone number suggests. Distinguish bone, cord segment and exiting root labels on the same diagram before predicting a neurological distribution.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Dorsal columns carry discriminative touch, vibration and conscious proprioception ipsilaterally to the medulla before crossing. Anterolateral pain-temperature pathways usually cross near entry over a few spinal segments. Most corticospinal fibers cross in the caudal medulla before descending in the lateral tract. A hemicord lesion therefore can combine ipsilateral motor and dorsal-column deficits with contralateral pain-temperature loss below the lesion. Cord segment and vertebral level diverge inferiorly because the vertebral column grows farther.
